name: HIIT

lead: HIIT alternates short, near-maximal bursts of exercise with brief recoveries, usually in sessions under 30 minutes. It is used as a time-efficient way to lose fat and build conditioning for a leaner physique.

Near-maximal efforts drive adaptations such as greater aerobic capacity, similar to longer moderate training. Meta-analyses find clear gains in cardiorespiratory fitness and cardiometabolic markers, with body-composition changes that are modest and generally similar to moderate continuous training in overweight adults.

paras: Users do rounds of hard efforts on a bike, rower, treadmill or sprints, separated by short rests, one to three times a week, often alongside lifting.
Injury, soreness and fatigue are reported; sustained overload may disturb hormones and sleep. People with heart conditions are advised to seek medical clearance first, per ACSM.

angle.text: Short all-out intervals burn calories and raise fitness, supporting fat loss and a leaner physique in little time. Trials show clear fitness gains, with fat-loss effects modest and similar to steady cardio.

lead: High-intensity interval training (HIIT) alternates short, near-maximal bursts of exercise with brief recovery periods, usually in sessions under 30 minutes. A related form, sprint interval training (SIT), uses all-out, supramaximal efforts.[1][2] People use it to lower body fat, build conditioning and get a leaner, more defined look in less training time than steady cardio typically takes; lower body fat is what makes existing muscle, jaw and facial structure more visible.[3][2]

Meta-analyses find that HIIT improves cardiorespiratory fitness and several cardiometabolic markers.[4][5][5] For body composition, a 2017 meta-analysis of 13 trials in overweight adults reported reductions in whole-body fat mass and waist circumference broadly similar to those from moderate continuous training, achieved with about 40% less training time.[3] A 2023 meta-analysis of 29 randomised trials in young and middle-aged adults found HIIT produced greater improvements than moderate continuous training in waist circumference, percent fat mass and peak oxygen uptake.[6]

The method has roots in track coaching in the 1930s to 1970s, entered exercise science with Izumi Tabata's 1996 study, spread through media such as the BBC Horizon programme in 2012, and now underlies group-fitness brands and bodybuilding contest preparation, where lifters ask how it compares with steady-state cardio for cutting body fat while keeping muscle.[2][7][8][9][10] Wikipedia notes it became a widely popular form of cardiovascular exercise in the 2010s.[2]
infobox: Sprint interval training, fartlek, high-intensity functional training [1][11][15]
Tabata, Gibala 60-second intervals, Norwegian 4x4, two-sprint 'Vollaard' routine [2]
Fitness, body composition, cardiometabolic markers, cardiac rehabilitation [4][5][3][26]
Orangetheory, CrossFit-style classes, boutique and app-based programmes [18][10]

paras: Work intervals are commonly 20 to 45 seconds and rarely exceed 75 seconds, separated by recovery periods; sessions typically finish in under 30 minutes.[2] Traditional HIIT was designed with efforts of no more than about 20 seconds and rests of no more than 10 seconds, and researchers distinguish HIIT (near-maximal efforts) from sprint interval training (supramaximal efforts over shorter bursts), although the two terms are not always kept distinct.[2][1] Both produce adaptations typical of moderate continuous training, such as increased aerobic capacity.[1]

Intervals can be done as running sprints, cycling, rowing, bodyweight circuits or group classes. Wikipedia distinguishes HIIT from the broader category of high-intensity functional training, which mixes resistance and aerobic movements.[2][11] Interval training in general can be varied by distance, recovery interval, repetitions and time, sometimes summarised as the 'DIRT' variables.[12]

Several named formats appear in the literature. In Tabata's 1996 experiment, seven participants trained five days a week for six weeks on a cycle ergometer, each session consisting of seven to eight 20-second bouts at about 170% of VO2max with 10-second rests; VO2max rose by about 7 ml/kg/min and anaerobic capacity by 28%, while a comparison group doing 60 minutes of moderate cycling five days a week raised VO2max from 53 to 58 ml/kg/min without a significant rise in anaerobic capacity.[13]

Martin Gibala's group at McMaster University published a protocol of 60-second efforts at about 95% of VO2max with 75 seconds of recovery, repeated 8 to 12 times, in 2010, and a gentler version for sedentary adults in 2011 using 60 seconds at 60% of peak power. Jorge Zuniga at Creighton University found that 30 seconds at 90% power with 30 seconds of rest gave the highest oxygen consumption and longest workout duration in his study. Niels Vollaard's group proposed a ten-minute routine containing two 20-second all-out sprints, and a 2017 meta-analysis found that 6 to 10 sprints of 30 seconds did not improve aerobic fitness more than this two-sprint protocol.[2] A 2011 study of 4 x 4, 4 x 8 and 4 x 16 minute intervals found the 4 x 8 format produced the largest VO2max gain, about 11% over seven weeks.[2]

A study comparing HIIT (eight 1-minute bouts at 85% of peak power) with SIT (eight 30-second bouts at 130%), time-matched at 24 minutes, found small differences between the two.[2] Gym-goers also combine intervals with lifting in circuit-style sessions and group classes, discussed below.

German coach Woldemar Gerschler (1904-1982) is described as a pioneer of interval training, using short runs at speeds that made race pace seem moderate and basing the approach on heart rates; he coached Rudolf Harbig to several world records in the 1930s, including the 800 metres in 1939.[14] In Sweden, coach Gosta Holmer developed fartlek ('speed play') in the late 1930s, mixing bursts of speed into a continuous run for the national cross-country team; the method reached the United States in the 1940s.[15] Emil Zatopek, who won the 5,000 m, 10,000 m and marathon at the 1952 Olympics, is credited with popularising interval training after the Second World War.[16]

In the 1970s Peter Coe had his son Sebastian run repeated fast 200 m efforts with about 30 seconds of recovery, drawing on ideas from Gerschler and from the Swedish physiologist Per-Olof Astrand.[2] Swimming coaches such as Soichi Sakamoto at the University of Hawaii and James Counsilman at Indiana were early advocates of interval training for swimmers.[12]

Tabata's 1996 paper, from Ritsumeikan University, tested a high-intensity intermittent protocol against steady training; the four-minute core of the session later became known as the Tabata protocol.[13][2] Talanian and colleagues reported in 2007 that seven HIIT sessions over two weeks improved fat oxidation in moderately active women, and Trapp's 2008 study found HIIT reduced fasting insulin by 31% versus 9% with moderate continuous training.[2]

Gibala's 2010 and 2011 protocols, Zuniga's 2011 study and Vollaard's 2012 proposal for a ten-minute routine followed.[2] In February 2012 the BBC Horizon programme 'The Truth About Exercise' had Jamie Timmons of Loughborough University lead presenter Michael Mosley through a three-sprint cycling routine performed three times a week; Mosley said he had gained improved insulin response from short, high-intensity sessions, and he co-wrote the 2013 book Fast Exercise.[2][17]

The HIIT idea was commercialised through group formats. CrossFit was conceived in 1996, incorporated in 2000, opened its first gym in Santa Cruz in 2001 and its first affiliate in Seattle in 2002, and grew from 13 affiliated gyms in 2005 to about 8,000 in 2013.[18] Orangetheory Fitness, founded in March 2010 by Ellen Latham, Jerome Kern and David Long in Fort Lauderdale, built one-hour classes around heart-rate zones and an 'afterburn' concept; it passed $1 billion in systemwide sales in 2018, had more than 1,500 studios by 2023 and merged with Anytime Fitness's parent in 2024.[10] Les Mills, a fitness-class company, is cited as having a 2012 CNN video titled 'Les Mills CEO: HIIT training popular'.[19]

HIIT recruits anaerobic energy pathways heavily, while aerobic pathways still contribute.[2] A 2017 review in The Journal of Physiology by MacInnis and Gibala compared HIIT, SIT and moderate continuous training for muscle mitochondria, VO2max, capillary density, cardiac function and blood volume: HIIT may increase mitochondrial content more than moderate training when work is matched, SIT increases it about as much as moderate training despite lower volume, and VO2max generally rises more with HIIT at matched volume, while evidence on capillary density, stroke volume, cardiac output and blood volume is sparse.[1] Wikipedia reports that aerobic work during HIIT is linked to a 20 to 30% increase in capillaries around muscle fibres.[2] A study in young and old adults found different exercise modes enhanced protein translation underlying metabolic and physical adaptations.[20]

Fitness marketing often refers to 'afterburn', which physiologists call excess post-exercise oxygen consumption (EPOC): oxygen use stays elevated after strenuous exercise as the body restores fuel stores, repairs tissue and clears heat. EPOC occurs after both aerobic and anaerobic exercise and rises with intensity; intermittent, higher-intensity exercise consistently produces a greater EPOC response than continuous exercise.[9] A 2004 review concluded that the EPOC from a single resistance session has little effect on energy balance, although its cumulative effect may be relevant.[9] One HIIT study found greater subcutaneous fat loss despite fewer calories burned during exercise, but its authors could not establish EPOC's role and diet was not controlled.[9] Orangetheory describes its orange and red heart-rate zones as the range in which EPOC may occur.[10]

A 2014 meta-analysis in people with lifestyle-induced cardiometabolic disease compared HIIT with moderate continuous training for fitness and safety; Wikipedia reports roughly a 19% VO2max increase with HIIT versus 10% with moderate training.[4][2] A review of 65 intervention studies found that, in overweight and obese adults, short-term HIIT (under 12 weeks) raised VO2max and lowered diastolic blood pressure and fasting glucose, and long-term HIIT (12 weeks or more) also reduced waist circumference, body fat percentage and resting heart rate; in normal-weight adults only VO2max improved.[5] A meta-analysis of HIIT and glucose regulation reported effects on insulin resistance, and Wikipedia cites an HbA1c reduction of 0.19% and 1.3 kg body-weight reduction versus controls.[21][2] A 2015 meta-analysis found effects on vascular function relative to moderate continuous training.[22]

A 2021 review of 66 trials (3,964 participants) with overweight or obese adults found all training types increased VO2max, with HIIT slightly more effective than aerobic training.[23] A review asked whether HIIT is a time-efficient strategy to improve health and fitness.[24]

A 2017 meta-analysis in Obesity Reviews screened 1,334 articles and included 13 trials (average ten weeks, three sessions per week) in overweight and obese adults aged 18 to 45. Both HIIT and moderate continuous training significantly reduced whole-body fat mass and waist circumference, neither outperformed the other, and HIIT needed about 40% less time. Running-based training had large effects on fat mass, with standardised mean differences of about -0.82 for HIIT and -0.85 for moderate training, while cycling did not produce fat loss in that analysis.[3]

The 2023 meta-analysis searched seven databases to October 2022, retrieved 1,738 studies and included 29 randomised trials. It reported that HIIT's effect on fat loss and cardiorespiratory fitness was similar to or better than moderate continuous training, noted that outcomes may depend on age (18-45), obesity, programme duration over six weeks, frequency and interval design, and found that fat-free mass did not change significantly within either group.[6] A network meta-analysis of 84 trials (4,836 participants) ranked vigorous aerobic exercise and HIIT highest for reducing visceral fat, weight, total body fat, BMI, waist circumference and subcutaneous fat in people with overweight or obesity.[25] Wikipedia describes the fat effect as modest in healthy people and larger in overweight people, with running-based HIIT effective against abdominal and visceral fat, and notes HIIT may be less effective than longer sessions for obesity or for building muscle and bone mass.[2]

Lifters often ask whether intervals preserve muscle better than long steady cardio. Controlled data are limited: the 2023 meta-analysis reported no significant change in fat-free mass in the HIIT or the moderate-training group,[6] and a 2021 study of 20 women reported that HIIT running and functional HIIT similarly reduced body fat and improved VO2max, while the functional format increased muscle strength more.[2] Trials that compare resistance training with and without interval work in lifters are not covered in the studies cited here.

Dozens of randomised trials and several meta-analyses exist. They show improved fitness and cardiometabolic markers and, for fat loss, effects broadly comparable to or somewhat larger than moderate continuous training, achieved in less time.[4][5][3][6] Trials have also examined HIIT in cardiac rehabilitation, including the FITR Heart randomised trial and a 382-patient multicentre trial, in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, and after stroke.[26][27][28][29] A 2025 trial in women with osteoporosis examined 16 weeks of HIIT with vitamin D on bone metabolism.[30] A network meta-analysis in children and adolescents with excess weight compared exercise modalities, including HIIT, for insulin-resistance markers.[31]

The American College of Sports Medicine advises consulting a doctor first, especially with a history of coronary heart disease.[2] Wikipedia reports that knees, shoulders and ankles are the most commonly injured sites and that high-intensity exercise can cause rapid blood-pressure spikes, which may risk hyper-perfusion injury in at-risk sedentary adults.[2]

Reported effects of overload include injury, acute stress responses such as elevated cortisol, higher resting heart rate, low mood and poorer sleep, which usually resolve within days to weeks with reduced intensity, and, with sustained overload, possible reductions in testosterone, thyroid function and bone density that can take weeks to months to resolve.[2] Some researchers question whether the general population can sustain the motivation HIIT demands.[2] Supervised HIIT has also been trialled in cardiac rehabilitation, including a multicentre randomised trial of 382 patients with coronary artery disease comparing low-volume HIIT with moderate steady-state training.[26]

A neighbouring high-intensity format, CrossFit, has had a public debate about injuries and rhabdomyolysis, a muscle-breakdown condition associated with high-volume, extreme-fatigue workouts. Critics say its methodology and culture raise risk, and CrossFit says its injury rates are comparable to general fitness training; a 2018 review reported injury rates comparable to or lower than several other sports.[18]

sections.h: Use in lifting and bodybuilding communities
paras: On T Nation, members discuss HIIT as a cutting tool alongside weights. One poster asked whether five HIIT classes a week was the right approach before a bulk; the thread was a request for feedback on a plan of fat loss with HIIT, then a calorie surplus with 5x5 lifting.[7] In a thread where members list lessons learned, one list included having tried HIIT for weight loss among earlier approaches the poster later reconsidered.[32] Another thread asks other competitors about experiences with different cardio forms for contest prep, including HIIT, bike and stairs.[8] A separate thread covers combining HIIT with powerlifting,[33] and a powerlifter in a home-gym thread says he throws in HIIT-style work such as box jumps and ball slams to round out athleticism.[34] A Hacker News submission about HIIT as an anti-ageing exercise drew 57 points in 2017, showing interest outside lifting circles.[35]

Related approaches include moderate-intensity continuous training (steady-state cardio), fartlek, hill repeats and other running intervals, sprint interval training, high-intensity functional training, circuit training with weights, and conditioning classes built on heart-rate zones.[1][2][11][12][15][10] Interval training combined with resistance training in adolescents was reported in a 2021 review to reduce waist size and body fat over 8 to 12 weeks.[2]

lore.intro: HIIT is commonly presented in fitness and bodybuilding communities as a fat-loss tool; T Nation threads ask how often to do it, how it fits with lifting and how it compares with other cardio for contest prep.[7][8][33]

claims.claim: HIIT burns fat faster than steady cardio.
A few minutes is enough to improve fitness.
HIIT can be done alongside lifting during a cut.
The 'afterburn effect' means HIIT keeps burning calories for hours after the session.
Four minutes of Tabata matches an hour of steady cardio.
HIIT preserves muscle better than long steady-state cardio.
Cycling and running intervals produce the same fat-loss results.
More HIIT sessions per week always gives better results.

timeline.event: Gosta Holmer develops fartlek, mixing speed bursts into continuous running, for Swedish cross-country runners.[15]
Woldemar Gerschler's athlete Rudolf Harbig sets an 800 m world record after interval-based training.[14]
Emil Zatopek wins the 5,000 m, 10,000 m and marathon at the Helsinki Olympics; he is credited with popularising interval training.[16]
Peter Coe has Sebastian Coe run repeated 200 m efforts with brief recovery.[2]
Tabata and colleagues publish a six-week study of intermittent cycle intervals; CrossFit is conceived the same year.[13][18]
Talanian and colleagues report improved fat oxidation after seven HIIT sessions in moderately active women.[2]
Gibala's McMaster group publishes a 60-second interval protocol; Orangetheory is founded in March.[2][10]
Gibala's gentler protocol for sedentary adults, Zuniga's 30:30 study and a 4 x 8-minute interval study (about 11% VO2max gain) appear.[2]
BBC Horizon features a three-sprint routine in February; Vollaard proposes a ten-minute two-sprint routine.[2]
Meta-analysis of HIIT in cardiometabolic disease reports about 19% versus 10% VO2max gains.[4][2]
Meta-analysis of 13 trials compares HIIT and moderate continuous training for body composition.[3]
A 29-trial meta-analysis finds HIIT similar or better than moderate training for fat loss and fitness; a 382-patient trial tests HIIT in cardiac rehabilitation.[6][26]
